profile.summary: 1 Peter is a pastoral and exhortation letter to Christians who suffered pressure, mockery and injustice because of faith. The central objective is to strengthen perseverance: suffering is not treated as a sign of abandonment, but as an occasion for maturation, witness and fidelity. The letter calls believers to live holyly, respectful and distinct from the surrounding culture, imitating Christ, who did not return when he was affronted. Instead of accommodation or retaliation, Peter points to the identity of the people of God, to the hope of salvation and to a lifestyle that glorifies God before a hostile world.
profile.setting: The letter was addressed to Christians in the Roman provinces of northern Asia Minor, a region now largely corresponding to Turkey. These believers lived under strong social pressure: they were seen as strangers, accused of improper conduct, criticized by their way of life and, in many cases, discriminated against not by aligning themselves with the prevailing customs of the Roman Empire. The source suggests that the conflict came mainly from society in general, sometimes with the support of local authorities, and not necessarily from official persecution of the state. As for authorship, the introduction identifies the apostle Peter; as for the place and date, it is understood that the letter was written from Rome, probably in the early 60s AD, but this is inferred from internal references and Christian tradition, not from direct external confirmation.

structure.label: Greeting and fundamentals of hope
structure.description: Identity of the recipients and basis to face the test with hope for the promised salvation.

structure.label: Holiness, new identity and people of God
structure.description: Called to live in holiness, love the brethren and recognize the status of people chosen and separated to God.

structure.label: Conduct before authorities and public testimony
structure.description: Exhortations to live respectfully under human authorities and respond to hostility with good and integrity.

structure.label: Suffering, vigilance and firmness
structure.description: New emphasis on perseverance amid trials and a sober life, faithful and God-centered.

structure.label: Final exhortations and closure
structure.description: Instructions to leaders, the younger and the church as a whole, followed by final greetings.

themes: perseverance in the midst of suffering
holiness and separation from the world
identity of the people of God
readingKeys: Notice how Peter connects present suffering to future hope and to the promised salvation.
Realize the repetition of calls for a holy life, respectful and full of good works.
Note the contrast between the surrounding culture and the identity of Christians as chosen and pilgrim people.
profile.cautions: The introduction does not present the letter as a response to an official persecution of the empire, but to social and local pressures; therefore, it is better to avoid readings that greatly simplify the context. There is also some implicit discussion about the place and date of composition: the source favors Rome and the early 1960s, but this is a reasonable inference, not an absolute certainty.

dossier.narratedEra: The letter places readers in the Roman world of the late 1st century BC and the 1st century AD, especially in the provinces of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, in the north of Asia Minor (now Turkey). The narrated scenario is that of Christians under pressure for social hostility, accusations, discrimination and sufferings (the ardent approvals), not necessarily by an official and state program of persecution. The text also presupposes the domestic and community life of churches in these provinces, with civil authorities, lords, husbands, elders and other believers as concrete interlocutors.
dossier.compositionEra: The tradition presented in the notes places the composition by Peter in Rome, probably in the early 60s, with the expression "Babylon" being understood as a symbolic reference to Rome. The notes also record Peter in Rome at the end of life according to Christian tradition, associated with martyrdom under Nero, probably in 64 or 65 AD. At the same time, Matthew Henry's introduction emphasizes Peter's traditional authorship and rejects the papal reading of his office, while Tyndale's notes treat Silas as the Amanuense of the letter.

politics.title: Roman provinces as official destination of the letter
politics.detail: The communities are located in Ponto, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, Roman provinces of northern Asia Minor. The letter takes on a real political-administrative space, not just an abstract hearing.
politics.readingImpact: This shows that the councils of submission, public conduct and testimony were given to Christians living within the Roman imperial order and under their local structures.

politics.title: Social hostage and court, more than formal imperial persecution
politics.detail: The notes describe the environment as ridicule, defamation, false accusations and discrimination on the part of the people and sometimes local authorities; the letter does not suggest an official state-run persecution program.
politics.readingImpact: This guides the reading of 1 Peter as a response to diffuse public and civic pressure, and not as a manual for a single centralized imperial persecution.

politics.title: Rome coded as "Babylon"
politics.detail: The expression "the church that is in Babylon" is almost certainly understood as a symbolic reference to the church in Rome. Babylon was small in the 1st century AD, but its name evoked the center of power hostile to the people of God, as in its symbolic use in Revelation.
politics.readingImpact: If read as a code for Rome, the final greeting suggests a Christian center within the empire and reinforces the tone of spiritual resistance to a world power.

politics.title: Nero and the tradition of Peter's martyrdom
politics.detail: Christian tradition places the end of Peter's life in Rome, where he would have suffered martyrdom under Emperor Nero, probably in 64 or 65 AD.
politics.readingImpact: This tradition helps to understand the pastoral weight of the letter: exhortations to suffer without retaliating gain strength when associated with the final context of Peter's apostolic life.
politics.reference: 1Pe 5:13 (with external tradition mentioned in the introduction)

politics.title: Public authorities as a sphere of testimony
politics.detail: The letter guides Christians to accept government authority and to live honorably before a hostile world.
politics.readingImpact: The central political theme is not revolution, but public conduct that witnesses Christ under recognized civil authority.

customs.title: Christian meetings seen as secret and suspicion
customs.detail: The notes say that in the ancient world Christians were regarded as strangers, superstitious and disloyal because they gathered in secret and practice misunderstood rites, like the Lord's Supper.
customs.readingImpact: The reading of 1 Peter should consider that the Christian faith was socially suspicious; therefore, the insistence on good public behavior functions as a practical apologetic defense.

customs.title: Refusal of oaths and military service as a cause of suspicion
customs.detail: Tyndale notes that Christians often refused to serve in the Roman army for not swearing allegiance to the emperor.
customs.readingImpact: This illuminates the conflict between fidelity to Christ and expectations of civic loyalty, helping to understand the pressure for cultural compliance.

customs.title: Long clothes and the language of mental readiness
customs.detail: In 1:13, clogging the loins of the mind is explained by the custom of sticking the bar of the long clothes on the belt to work or run.
customs.readingImpact: The image communicates urgency and practical disposition; it is not moral abstraction, but active readiness in the face of suffering and hope.

customs.title: Patriarchal House and Domestic duties
customs.detail: The exhortations to wives, husbands, servants and young men show an ancient domestic structure in which male authority and family hierarchy were culturally expected. The notes highlight husbands as the head of the relationship and wives, especially with pagan husbands, as called to a persevering testimony.
customs.readingImpact: Reading must see that the letter speaks within the real domestic arrangements of the Greco-Roman world, without idealizing them; obedience appears as a missionary and ethical strategy under pressure.

customs.title: Honor in marriage and social fragility of women
customs.detail: The notes claim that the wife was often physically weaker and socially less able to impose himself in that society, and that the husband had a duty to protect and honor his wife. It is also noted that submission aimed, in particular, married wives with unbelievers who could be hostile to the Christian faith.
customs.readingImpact: This prevents simplistic reading of the text: admonition is not only about domestic order, but about care, honor and testimony in an unequal social context.

customs.title: Greeting with kissing love and community communion
customs.detail: The closure mentions a "blove kiss," treated as a Christian custom of fraternal greeting.
customs.readingImpact: The end of the letter is not only formal; it shows concrete communion between members of the church, in contrast to external hostility.

language.title: dispersion expressions as an identity metaphor
language.detail: Tyndale explains that "exilados" describes someone torn from the homeland; Peter uses the image metaphorically to say that Christians live in a world dominated by anti-Christian values.
language.readingImpact: Language shifts the identity of readers: they belong to God, but they live as foreigners, which supports the ethics of moral separation without physical escape.

language.title: New birth as a frame of the letter
language.detail: The "birth again" is described as a way of speaking of Christian conversion, and the same word reappears in 1:23, framing the beginning of the section.
language.readingImpact: This makes 1 Peter a letter about renewed identity before it is only a manual of suffering; the behavior flows from the new life received.

language.title: Inheritance, salvation, and future temporality
language.detail: The inheritance is explained how the spiritual benefit and eternal salvation promised by God; the final salvation will be revealed in the time of Christ.
language.readingImpact: Language shifts the focus of the hostile present into the guaranteed future, strengthening the perseverance of readers.

language.title: The Proven Gold and the Tested Faith
language.detail: Faith is compared to gold refined by the test; the point is that suffering reveals the genuineness of faith.
language.readingImpact: Suffering is not presented as failure, but as a means of purification and proof of faith before God.

language.title: sacrificial language: rescue and lamb without defect
language.detail: Redemption is described as the ransom of captives, and Christ is called the undefective Lamb, in parallel with the Passover.
language.readingImpact: The letter interprets the work of Christ in categories of liberation and sacrifice; this lays the foundation for the required holiness of the readers.

language.title: Debate on the "spirits in prison."
language.detail: The notes present three readings for 3:19-20: preaching to the dead, preaching of Christ through Noah, or proclamation of victory over evil spiritual beings. The third is pointed out as the most likely in the comment.
language.readingImpact: The passage should be read with caution; its main function, according to the note, is to reinforce Christ's victory and encourage persecuted believers not to fear spiritual powers.

timeline.title: Destiny of churches in Asia Minor at the beginning of Christian witness
timeline.detail: The letter is addressed to communities scattered throughout five Roman provinces of Asia Minor, probably covered by a messenger following a route of circulation of the letter.
timeline.readingImpact: This suggests a network of churches connected to each other, not a single isolated congregation, which helps to read exhortations as circular instructions.

timeline.title: Peter in Jerusalem, Judea, and then another place
timeline.detail: Tyndale's introduction notes that there is little information about Peter's movements after Acts 1-12; after being released from prison, he was "to another place."
timeline.readingImpact: This gap makes it possible, but not demonstrable from the letter, its later presence outside of Judea; the letter does not depend on a detailed biography.
timeline.reference: At 12:17 (mentioned in the introduction of the source)

timeline.title: Peter at the council of Jerusalem and Antioch/Krinth
timeline.detail: The introduction mentions his presence at the council of Jerusalem and apparently in Corinth and Antioch at some point.
timeline.readingImpact: These milestones explain the apostolic circulation, but do not prove that Peter had been in the provinces assigned to the letter.

timeline.title: Composition in Rome and the reference to "Babylon"
timeline.detail: The letter was probably written from Rome; the note states that "Babylon" is almost certainly a symbolic name for Rome. The presence of Mark with Peter is used as a support to situate the writing at the end of the apostle's life.
timeline.readingImpact: The final greeting gains historical density: the church writes from the imperial center, but under codified name, which reinforces the prudent and pastoral character of the letter.

timeline.title: Beginning of the 60s AD as a probable date
timeline.detail: If the letter came from Rome and whether Mark was with Peter, the introduction concludes that 1 Peter was probably written in the early 1960s.
timeline.readingImpact: This date places the letter near the period when hostility to Christians was already socially intense, without requiring the text to depend on a specific imperial decree.

timeline.title: Martyrdom of Peter under Nero, probably 64-65 AD
timeline.detail: The Christian tradition mentioned in the introduction places Peter's death in Rome under Emperor Nero, probably in 64 or 65 AD.
timeline.readingImpact: If accepted as a traditional background, this data deepens the reading of the letter as a testimony of perseverance in the face of extreme suffering.
timeline.reference: No direct biblical reference at the source; tradition linked to authorship

investigation: Tyndale's source discusses in great detail the social suffering of Christians, but does not identify a specific state persecution; therefore, any attempt to date the letter by a concrete imperial event is beyond what the text provided sustains.
Matthew Henry insists on petrine authorship and its value to instruct newly converted and prepare them for suffering, but does not offer fine historical data on the social setting of Asian provinces.
The notes provided unequally cover chapters: there is more explanation for 1:1-25, 3:1'22 and 5:1'14 than for other passages, so that the above items reflect this selectivity.
The identification of "Babylon" with Rome, the presence of Mark and the dating in the early 1960s are editorial inferences of the notes, not independent proofs.
The discussion of 3:19-20 is explicitly discussed; the dossier records the alternatives presented without choosing beyond what the note itself favors.

There is not enough information in the attached sources to reconstruct in detail local economy, calendars, civic parties or urban structures specific to the aforementioned provinces; therefore, these aspects have not been expanded beyond what is directly mentioned.
dossier.limits: This dossier uses only the attached notes and therefore depends on the interpretative clipping of the commentators. There is strong coverage of suffering, Christian identity, domestic authority and the symbolic identification of Babylon with Rome, but there is little information on fine chronology, provincial administration, regional economics and detailed daily customs. The statements about petrine authorship, Rome, Mark and the date in the early 1960s appear as traditional inferences of the sources, not as independent historical proof. There are also really debated issues, especially 1Pe 3:19-20, in which the notes present three possible readings. In line with the Protestant evangelical perspective of these sources, the focus is on pastoral exhortation and canonical coherence, but without dealing with traditional interpretations as automatically demonstrated by history.
